analysis.one_liner: Makes drug makers refund Medicare for discarded amounts of single-dose vial drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one Democrat with one Republican cosponsor, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Many Medicare drugs come in single-dose vials sized larger than what a patient needs, and hospitals bill Medicare for the leftover amount that gets thrown away. This bill would make the drug manufacturers, not taxpayers, refund Medicare for most of that discarded medicine each quarter, with the refunds deposited into the Medicare trust fund. Manufacturers that don't pay would face a civil penalty on top of what they owe. The bill was introduced in April 2021 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers, because the Medicare trust fund would stop paying drug makers for medicine that is thrown away, and the savings would help keep the fund solvent.

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers of single-dose vial drugs paid for under Medicare Part B to refund the government for discarded amounts, replacing the current practice of billing Medicare for the waste.
Sets the refund at 90 percent of the value of the discarded units, with amounts deposited into the Federal Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund.
Imposes a civil money penalty on manufacturers who fail to pay, equal to what they owe plus 25 percent, and requires audits of both manufacturers and providers.

Directs the HHS Inspector General to report to Congress on how the refunds affect biosimilar competition and manufacturers' vial sizes and labeling, giving lawmakers a way to check the policy's side effects.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers whose single-dose vials and single-use packages are billed to Medicare Part B, which would repay the government quarterly for discarded doses.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers selling to Medicare

drawbacks.text: The refund only targets waste in billing, not the underlying product sizes: manufacturers could respond by changing vial sizes or prices, and the bill requires a study of those effects on biosimilar market entry rather than preventing them.

Some discarded amounts come from FDA-approved preparation steps, such as drugs that must be filtered with the unused portion thrown away; the bill recognizes this and lets the Secretary adjust the refund percentage for those drugs, acknowledging the policy does not fit every product neatly.
Radiopharmaceuticals and imaging agents are excluded entirely, so waste in those products would remain billable to Medicare.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit is real but modest: Medicare stops paying drug makers for medicine that is discarded, and taxpayers keep that money in the trust fund. The main costs are administrative and the risk that manufacturers restructure vial sizes or pricing to recoup the refunds, which the bill monitors through an Inspector General report rather than solving in advance. The carve-out for imaging and radiopharmaceutical drugs narrows the savings. On balance the policy would save Medicare money, but the amounts depend heavily on how manufacturers respond.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 117th Congress ended without any committee vote or floor action.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on April 21, 2021, together with Senator Portman, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
Its one cosponsor was Senator Portman, a Republican, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship from the start.
The complete action history shows no further steps after the referral: no committee vote, no report, and no floor action.

The bill would have required drug manufacturers to issue quarterly refunds to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services for discarded amounts of single-dose vial drugs covered by Medicare, with civil penalties for noncompliance.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without the bill ever reaching a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept collecting Medicare payment for the portion of single-dose vials that providers discard, and the Medicare trust fund never received the refunds the bill would have generated.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers selling single-dose vials

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat (Durbin) sponsored the bill with a Republican (Portman) as its sole cosponsor, and no votes were ever taken, so the fight never took a partisan shape.

industries.industry: Brand-name drug makers (single-source drugs and biologics)
industries.note: These manufacturers would repay Medicare 90 percent of the value of discarded single-dose vial amounts each quarter, ending a practice in which providers bill Medicare for the waste. Their savings would otherwise come out of the Medicare trust fund that taxpayers and beneficiaries fund.

The bill explicitly excludes these products from the refund requirement, so Medicare would keep paying for discarded amounts of them. The carve-out means waste in these drugs stays on the public's tab.

The bill directs a government study of whether the refunds affect biosimilar market entry, since manufacturers might change vial sizes or pricing in ways that discourage lower-cost competition. Cheaper biosimilars would benefit patients, so preserving their market entry runs alongside the public's interest.
